pronunciation.note: Benzaiten is Tier 2: the Japanese form is plain Hepburn. The name is a Sino-Japanese Buddhist import; its distinctiveness lies in cultural history, not in orthography.

domains.title: Goddess of Music, Wealth, and Eloquence
domains.subtitle: One of the Seven Gods of Fortune
domains.lead: Benzaiten is the Japanese transformation of Sarasvatī, the Indian goddess of rivers, speech, and learning. In Japan she became one of the Seven Gods of Fortune (Shichifukujin), patron of music, eloquence, and wealth, and she is worshipped at island shrines, especially Enoshima and Chikubushima, where land and water meet.

cards.name: Biwa Musician
cards.desc: She is depicted playing the lute-like biwa, master of sound and persuasive speech.

cards.name: Seven Gods of Fortune
cards.desc: The only woman among the Shichifukujin, she brings luck to artists and merchants.

cards.name: Island Patron
cards.desc: Her shrines stand on islands and lakeshores, where water, speech, and commerce converge.

cards.name: Serpent Companion
cards.desc: In Japan she is often accompanied by a snake or dragon, guardians of treasure.

mythology.lead: Benzaiten's mythology weaves together Indian river-goddess lore, Chinese Buddhist translation, and Japanese folk religion.

myths.title: From Sarasvatī to Benzaiten
myths.text: In India, Sarasvatī was first a river and then a goddess of speech, learning, and the arts. Buddhist texts carried her name eastward, where Chinese translators rendered her as Biancaitian, 'Goddess of Eloquent Speech.' In Japan the name softened into Benzaiten, and her domain expanded to include wealth, music, and maritime fortune.

myths.title: The Serpent of Enoshima
myths.text: A famous legend tells of a five-headed dragon that plagued the coast near Enoshima. Benzaiten descended from India, subdued the dragon, and made the island her dwelling. The dragon became her protector, and Enoshima became one of her most important cult centers, drawing pilgrims who sought safety at sea and prosperity on land.

myths.title: Island and Lake Shrines
myths.text: Benzaiten's major shrines are on islands and lakes: Enoshima in Sagami Bay, Chikubushima in Lake Biwa, and Itsukushima in the Inland Sea. These liminal locations reflect her origins as a water goddess and her role as guardian of fishermen, sailors, and merchants.

lore.syncretism: Benzaiten is a layered deity. Her root is Indian Sarasvatī, her skin is Chinese Biancaitian, and her Japanese form absorbed Shinto water-kami and dragon lore. She appears in both Buddhist and Shinto contexts, often paired with Ebisu as a fortune couple, and in the Edo period she became a fixture of popular prints and merchant devotion.
lore.culturalLegacy: Benzaiten remains one of Japan's most popular fortune deities. Her image appears on New Year prints, in manga and anime, and at shrines where artists and business owners pray for success. Enoshima's Hetsunomiya Shrine continues to draw millions.
lore.extendedMeditation: Benzaiten reminds us that wealth and eloquence flow like water. Speech can persuade, music can move, and both are forms of prosperity. She is the goddess of graceful influence.

lore.archaeology: Benzaiten's most prominent shrines are at Enoshima (Kanagawa) and Chikubushima (Lake Biwa). Both sites preserve Edo-period shrine architecture, statuary, and votive materials documenting her popularity among fishermen, merchants, and performers.
